cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: we would give these tools to an expert and they would get great results
cards.claim: RPI worked for expert users but results degraded when handed to their teams, so tool design must not depend on expert skill.
cards.evidence_detail: Thousands of engineers from startups to Fortune 500 since Oct 2025; no numbers.
cards.landing: Phase routine: design for the fresh agent, not the author; informs P1 cold-resume trial

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: good research is all facts, but if you tell the model what you're building, then you get opinions
cards.claim: Research must be fed no description of the feature, or it returns opinions instead of facts.
cards.evidence_detail: Observed across rollouts; no measurement.
cards.landing: Research/diagnosis step of phase routine; knowledge-store diagnoses; Workflow explorer prompts

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: we just hide the ticket from the context window that's doing research
cards.claim: Step Q/R: one context generates questions from the ticket, then a fresh context with no knowledge of the goal answers them, done deterministically.
cards.evidence_detail: Described as a trivial query-planning analogue; no results given.
cards.landing: Workflow script (questions agent then blind researcher); fixflow-explorer agent usage

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Keep things objective. Discourage opinions. Don't actually put any implementation details in there.
cards.claim: Research output should compress only what is true about how the code works today, with no implementation detail.
cards.evidence_detail: Restates the November 2025 research rule.
cards.landing: Research/explorer agent prompt; knowledge-store entry template (facts only)

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: a single giant like monolithic thing with 85 or more instructions
cards.claim: The RPI planning prompt held 85+ instructions including interactive steps, and about half of users saw the agent skip them and write the plan outright.
cards.evidence_detail: 85+ instruction count; skip rate stated as 'about 50% of people, maybe more'.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md length (W1); any phase routine step that is only a prose instruction

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you have to say the magic words
cards.claim: If a tool only works when the user says magic words, the tool is broken and must be fixed so the correct behaviour is the default.
cards.evidence_detail: Workshop experience; the 'work back and forth with me' line separated good from bad plans.
cards.landing: Phase routine: make steps structural (separate step/script) rather than reminders in chat

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: frontier LLMs could only follow about 150 to 200 instructions with like good consistency
cards.claim: Models follow only about 150-200 instructions reliably, and the budget is shared by the prompt, CLAUDE.md, system prompt, tools and MCP.
cards.evidence_detail: Cited from an arXiv paper via Kyle's blog; Dex says the number is probably higher now (2026).
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md trim (390 lines); skill and agent sizing; per-phase prompt budget

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you're not likely to get full adherence to the workflow
cards.claim: Stacking an 85-instruction prompt on top of CLAUDE.md, system prompt, tools and MCP means workflow adherence is a dice roll.
cards.evidence_detail: Inference from the instruction-budget number.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md always-loaded content vs on-demand skills

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: a thousand line plan tends to be about a thousand lines of code within 10%
cards.claim: Reading a long plan saves no work since the plan is as long as the code and the code can differ from it, so do not review long plans.
cards.evidence_detail: Rule of thumb 'within 10% or so'; no study.
cards.landing: Opus reviewer per PR: review code and diff, not the plan; owner view page length

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: We tried not reading the code for like 6 months. It did not end well.
cards.claim: Dex reverses his August 2025 advice: engineers must read the code, as six months without reading forced rip-and-replace of large parts of HumanLayer's system.
cards.evidence_detail: Own team experience; no numbers.
cards.landing: Reviewer and owner-view design; human read of diffs for money/lifecycle invariants

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Nobody gets paged at 3:00 a.m. if it's broken
cards.claim: Projects whose maintainers skip reading code (Beads, OpenClaw) are OSS with low stakes, so they are not a model for production or regulated code.
cards.evidence_detail: Argument by stakes; cites Beads 300,000 lines.
cards.landing: Risk-tiered review depth (money, auth, dispatcher paths get human read)

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: going 10 times faster doesn't matter if you're going to throw it all away
cards.claim: Against agent swarms and Gas Town style speed: target a 2-3x speedup at near-human quality rather than 10x with slop.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated as a goal; measurement left to another talk.
cards.landing: Ship-plan pacing: one phase per session, quality gate over throughput

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: there is no magic prompt. Do not outsource the thinking.
cards.claim: Principles he kept: no magic prompt, do not outsource the thinking, and seek leverage so correctness can be assured without reading everything and re-steering afterwards.
cards.evidence_detail: Credits Jake from Netflix for 'do not outsource the thinking'.
cards.landing: Owner view and decisions journal: human decisions captured before code

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the less of the context window you use, the better results you will get
cards.claim: The dumb zone: quality degrades from about 40% of a 168k usable window on average, and more MCP tools mean more unused instructions in context.
cards.evidence_detail: ~40% average threshold, 60% still workable; cites Databricks on too many MCPs.
cards.landing: One-phase-per-session rule; context budget guidance; MCP/tool trimming

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Don't use prompts for control flow if you can use control flow for control flow.
cards.claim: Classify the input and route it to small focused prompts rather than one prompt with if-branches; true of any LLM system.
cards.evidence_detail: Follows 12-factor agents; 85 instructions became all under 40 per step.
cards.landing: Workflow scripts as the control-flow layer for the phase routine; skills per step

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: before it was 85 instructions, now they're all less than 40
cards.claim: Splitting the monolith into per-step prompts brought each below 40 instructions, with some likely reducible further.
cards.evidence_detail: Instruction counts 85+ to under 40 per prompt; still iterating.
cards.landing: Per-skill instruction cap; trim target for CLAUDE.md

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: we figured it was time to actually go drink our own Kool-Aid
cards.claim: He admits HumanLayer wrote the 12-factor 'no monolith' advice then built a monolithic prompt around Claude Code anyway.
cards.evidence_detail: Self-critique.
cards.landing: Reminder that skills/agents beat one long routine

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: questions, research, design, structure, plan, work tree, implement, PR
cards.claim: QRSPI is a seven-to-eight step pipeline: Questions, Research, Design, Structure, Plan, Worktree, Implement, PR, each its own fresh context and artifact.
cards.evidence_detail: Steps spoken in talk; acronym picked from steps he liked (CRISPY).
cards.landing: Phase routine decomposition; a saved Workflow with one step per stage

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Here's the current state, the desired end state. It has the patterns to follow.
cards.claim: Step D (design discussion, ~200 lines): current state, desired end state, patterns to follow, resolved decisions and open questions in one editable markdown artifact.
cards.evidence_detail: 200 lines versus a 1,000-line plan; no measured outcome.
cards.landing: Draft PR body 'Plan @ sha' plus decisions journal; knowledge-store entry

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: that's not how we do atomic SQL updates. That's some engineer that doesn't work here
cards.claim: The design step is the chance to correct which codebase patterns the agent found, rejecting legacy ones before it copies them.
cards.evidence_detail: Illustrative example.
cards.landing: Pattern pointers (e.g. try_claim / try_transition) in the design/plan artifact rather than CLAUDE.md prose

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you can do brain surgery on the agent before you proceed downstream
cards.claim: Force the agent to dump what it found, intends and assumes, and ask questions, so the human can correct it before 2,000 lines are written.
cards.evidence_detail: Credits Matt Pocock's 'design concept'.
cards.landing: Owner approval gate on the plan before code; refuter reads the design artifact

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: if the plan is the implementation, the outline is the C header files
cards.claim: Step S (structure outline, ~2 pages vs 8-page plan): phases, signatures, new types, order of change and test points, as a cheap review artifact.
cards.evidence_detail: Plan eight pages vs outline two pages for the same feature.
cards.landing: Phase plan format in ship plan; PR body structure

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: we cannot get models to stop writing horizontal plans
cards.claim: Models write horizontal plans (all DB, then services, API, UI) despite heavy prompting and evals; vertical slices with checkpoints are the fix and the outline step is where they are enforced.
cards.evidence_detail: 'prompt this out and eval the hell out of this'; horizontal plans reach 1,200 lines with nothing testable.
cards.landing: Per-phase fail-before/pass-after checkpoints; slice-ordered phases across backend/web/mobile

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I don't actually test in between every phase everything I'm building
cards.claim: Test checkpoints between phases are for sensitive, hard or complex work, aiming for 200-400 line blocks verified before more code.
cards.evidence_detail: Personal practice; block size 'two, three, 400 line'.
cards.landing: Verifier intensity by risk tier; block-size guidance

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: this is a tactical doc for the agent. ... I'm just going to spot-check this
cards.claim: Step P: once design and outline are aligned the plan is only spot-checked and deep review is saved for the code.
cards.evidence_detail: Same template and prompt as create_plan.
cards.landing: Reviewer effort allocation: code-heavy, plan-light

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: any of my bad decisions are headed off on a 200-line doc
cards.claim: Send short design docs to the code owner before coding (optional, not a required step) so code review confirms rather than discovers.
cards.evidence_detail: HumanLayer practice; co-founder is code owner.
cards.landing: Owner view page sent before the build starts; decisions journal in draft PR

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: it's still a 2-day feature cuz I still have to like align with my team
cards.claim: Coding is 2-4 hours of a 2-day feature, so AI on coding alone barely moves cycle time; alignment, review and verification dominate and AI should help there.
cards.evidence_detail: Illustrative arithmetic (coding 20 minutes).
cards.landing: Spend verifier/effort budget on alignment and verification, not generation

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Igor ... shipping 50% more, but half of that is just cleaning up the slop
cards.claim: Cites Stanford study numbers: AI raises output ~50% but half is rework, good for low-complexity greenfield and poor for high-complexity brownfield.
cards.evidence_detail: Last year's numbers pre-Opus 4.5; he says to inflate them a little.
cards.landing: Motivation for refuter-first review; baseline for measuring rework

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: three steps is already a lot for some people to learn and now there are seven
cards.claim: Open problems he names: seven steps is heavy to adopt, impact on teams is unmeasured, and updating shared prompts/skills without regressing other teams is unsolved.
cards.evidence_detail: Listed as not yet addressed.
cards.landing: Skill versioning and regression-test question for .claude/skills; saved workflow library

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: we don't use the built-in compaction because everything that matters is going into static assets
cards.claim: Skip built-in compaction: persist all that matters to markdown artifacts so any session can resume without relying on compact quality.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated in Q&A as HumanLayer practice.
cards.landing: One phase per new session; P1 cold-resume trial; knowledge store

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I will regularly go up to 60. I will regularly like aggressively keep it below 30.
cards.claim: Experienced users treat the dumb zone loosely (30 to 60%), but novices should aim under 40% and wrap up near 60%, iterating on the same doc.
cards.evidence_detail: Personal practice after 60 h/week use; teaching default of 40/60.
cards.landing: Context budget thresholds in the phase routine (wrap-up trigger)

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: we're binary searching through the space of how much of the code should you read
cards.claim: The right amount of code reading is still being searched for; those saying never read will likely reverse, and reading code with 2-3x speed beats 10x slop.
cards.evidence_detail: Q&A answer; predicts a reversal in six months.
cards.landing: Reviewer policy: sampled vs full read by risk

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Let's put it that way. I do not endorse that.
cards.claim: He rejects the software-factory stance where no human reads code and the spec is the source, including formal verification (TLA+) as a replacement for now.
cards.evidence_detail: Q&A reply to a StrongDM-style question; says more verification tooling remains to be built.
cards.landing: Verifier strategy: do not drop human read in favour of spec-only verification

cards.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Testing and verifying, sorry, I don't have a good answer for you.
cards.claim: He explicitly leaves testing/verification out of QRSPI's scope, deferring to another speaker.
cards.evidence_detail: Admission of a gap.
cards.landing: Gap note: QRSPI does not supply a verifier design

cards.source_title: What's Missing to Make AI Agents Mainstream?
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: our implementer agent uses faster, smaller models for writing the code and running the tests
cards.claim: Implementer sub-agent uses a small fast model to write code and run tests while a larger model spot-checks, keeping the parent context low for re-steering.
cards.evidence_detail: Described HumanLayer practice; no cost numbers.
cards.landing: Model routing per agent file (cheap implementer, strong spot-checker); effort routing

cards.source_title: What's Missing to Make AI Agents Mainstream?
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you always get better results if you use less of them
cards.claim: No matter how large context windows get, using less context gives better results, and deciding how to use less is the engineer's job.
cards.evidence_detail: Repeated principle; refers to his testing-feedback blog on deterministic failure signals instead of full test dumps.
cards.landing: Backpressure scripts that return only failures; capped outputs

cards.source_title: What's Missing to Make AI Agents Mainstream?
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I don't know if I actually recommend that people should use Ralph to write production software.
cards.claim: Ralph loops are valuable for the context-engineering lessons, not as a production technique; techniques will not last six months.
cards.evidence_detail: Interview opinion.
cards.landing: Do not adopt loop-until-done automation for production phases; keep fresh-session discipline

cards.source_title: What's Missing to Make AI Agents Mainstream?
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Match the format of this code we found in the codebase in this other file
cards.claim: LLMs excel at finding and following patterns, so surface all applicable codebase patterns and let humans choose old versus new before coding.
cards.evidence_detail: Interview reasoning for the design step.
cards.landing: Pattern catalogue as retrievable knowledge-store items instead of CLAUDE.md prose

cards.source_title: What's Missing to Make AI Agents Mainstream?
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: once you get to know what the input space would be, you can give people a happy path
cards.claim: Decompose a workflow into a reliable happy path once the input space is known, with an escape hatch to a free-running LLM for the unexpected; choose your place on the autonomy slider.
cards.evidence_detail: Interview opinion.
cards.landing: Saved workflows for recurring phase types with an explicit eject-to-human path

cards.source_title: The Humans in the Loop Deep Dive reprint
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Under the hood, we were fundamentally helping people do better context engineering
cards.claim: RPI had no magic; the value was context engineering, and the team is productizing collaboration features around coding agents.
cards.evidence_detail: Product framing (Google Docs/Figma-like collaboration); reprint of Heavybit text with no new material.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious

cards.source_title: Alex Lavaee: From RPI to QRSPI
cards.author: other
cards.quote: The framework grew from 3 steps to 8. That's added complexity
cards.claim: Critique: QRSPI adds ceremony, and if the workflow needs too much ceremony engineers will skip steps and return to the original problems.
cards.evidence_detail: Reports community pushback; no data. Also states eight stages while Dex's talk and interview say seven.
cards.landing: Risk that the 40-phase routine is skipped; keep routine step count small

cards.source_title: agent-brain wiki: QRSPI concept page
cards.author: other
cards.quote: Question, Research, Spec, Plan, Implement
cards.claim: Critique of fidelity: the wiki expands the acronym differently (Spec for Design, five steps, drops Structure and Worktree), showing the framework is easily misreported secondhand.
cards.evidence_detail: Compare talk: Questions, Research, Design, Structure, Plan, Worktree, Implement, PR.
cards.landing: Use the primary talk only; do not rely on secondary summaries when copying QRSPI

gaps: Podwise page was only a third-party summary and outline; talk content taken from the YouTube transcript, an auto-caption with possible mis-hearings such as 'Beats' for Beads.
Heavybit article page and Humans in the Loop reprint share identical text, so no separate cards were made for the reprint beyond one marketing card.

Follow-on pages were read only for critique cards; only two critique cards were possible. Lavaee's content is mostly restatement and cites a 40/60 context rule that Dex's talk gives as 40 for novices and 60 for experts.
The transcript does not state the venue, and the talk was not checked against the slides; slide-only content such as the 12 factor agents graphics is not captured.
Recorded date 2026-03-03 taken from the bundle notes; card source_date uses it for the talk and publication dates for the articles.
